name: Zoe Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Zoe, thanks for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Ready when you are.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ready! I've been waiting for someone to ask me about this, to be honest. I think about it pretty much every day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Then let's start simple. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do Portuguese-English localisation for small game studios and a couple of apps. Localisation means making the game feel like it was written in your language: menus, item names, jokes, the dialogue of a grumpy blacksmith. I run everything through an AI draft first, then I rewrite it so it actually sounds human. My friend Inês and I share a tiny two-person collective, so we split bigger projects and check each other's work over video calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love naming things. Last month I had to translate a potion called 'Sopa de Pedra', stone soup, and make the joke land in English. What wears me out is studios that send ten thousand lines on a Friday and want them Monday. I'm still not as good as Inês at keeping a character's voice the same across a whole game, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? That'd be a bit disappointing. I like the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a nice spellchecker with ambitions, and humans still make games feel alive. I'd post a meme about it on the localisation forum. Everyone would laugh because we'd all be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be great for me. I'm already faster than most juniors because I use the AI drafts well, so a plateau keeps that edge without the studios replacing us. My rent comes from the little flat my aunt left me, so my money's solid either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and keep building my own setup: the glossary that feeds the AI draft, the style sheets for each character. I'd probably package that setup and sell it to other freelancers as a template for twenty or thirty a go. And I'd take on one more studio client, since I'd have the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a bit bored by how calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the flat makes your money solid. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt left me a one-bedroom flat in the town where I grew up, and I rent it out. That covers my own rent here, almost exactly. Having my aunt's little flat paying my rent means I can say yes to weird, fun projects instead of just the safe ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The translators who refused the tools completely. In a plateau they're okay, but they're slower, so studios still pay them less. I'd tell them it's not a moral choice to use a better dictionary.

Humans still make **games feel alive**, and we'd all be relieved.
think: My **AI drafts** already make me faster than most juniors.
A plateau keeps my **edge** without studios replacing translators.
Rent from my **aunt's flat** keeps my money solid either way.

Sell her setup as a **template** to freelancers for twenty or thirty each.

fieldNote: She's an **early adopter** who already treats AI as her first draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ooh. Okay, that's the realistic one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators need to be credited in games and paid fairly for fixing AI work, and I'd back a game workers' union. I'd post a long thread about it. Probably several long threads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the bottom of my market goes first. A small studio can run its own AI draft and skip people like me for item names and menus. I think the work left is the hard part: voice, humour, culture, checking that a joke doesn't offend someone in Brazil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell myself as a localisation quality lead, not a translator: the person who checks the whole game feels right in Portuguese. I'd learn the studios' own AI tools inside out so they hire me to run them. And I'd join the game workers' union branch that's forming, and push for credits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit fizzy. It's scary and exciting at the same time. I'm better placed than most, and I feel a bit guilty saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're junior and still learning, by your own account. Why would studios trust you as a quality lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question, and it keeps me up sometimes. My friend Inês is better at voice than me. But I'm better than her at the tools, so maybe we sell ourselves as a pair, her ear and my setup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the money if the small jobs dry up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose maybe a quarter of my income for a while. The flat rent covers my rent, so I'd eat into savings for food and fun, not for keeping a roof over my head.

I'd back a **game workers' union** and post long threads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Two years. That's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a public income floor, and we need it now, not after half the creative jobs are gone. I'd be loud about it online, and I'd go to the protests. I'd also say AI companies should pay into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 nobody pays me to localise anything, quality lead or not, because the AI does voice and humour too. My skills are thinking work, so I get the full hit on day one. The only good bit is the robots coming about three years later, so in-person work survives a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start planning a board-game café with Inês right away, because that's people, tables and coffee, not screens. I'd put about half my savings into it and use the flat rent as our safety net. I'd also stop all big spending this year, no new laptop, no trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in my chest. But I'm the type who has to do something with that feeling, so the café plan helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A café in 2028 with robots coming in 2031. How long do you think it lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the robots can make coffee by then, sure. But people come to a board-game café to sit with other people and have someone explain the rules with a bit of drama. I'm betting people still want a human who loses badly at a board game with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would say I wasted my degree. I'd tell my mum my degree taught me how people talk to each other, and a café is just that with snacks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That gives me some runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about an income floor, but I'd add that five years is enough to plan properly if governments start now. I'd want the union to run training for game workers moving into other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd squeeze localisation hard for three or four years, because the tools would make me fast and the money would still be there. Then I'd be out by 2031, with savings and a plan. The café would get the three years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep localising and use every AI tool going, so I can take on more projects and save more, maybe 800 a month. I'd test the café idea with pop-up game nights in a bar on Thursdays, starting next year. And I'd take a short business course so I don't sink the money stupidly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy, plotting kind of way. Less in my chest, more in my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pop-up game nights tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether people pay to play with strangers, and whether Inês and I can stand running something together on a Thursday after a full week. If ten people come back three weeks in a row, that's a yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd squeeze the work hard. Is that a bit contradictory with your union talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is. I'd be using the same tools that push other translators out, and I'm not going to pretend I'm not taking the money while it's there. I'd still pay my union dues and fight for them, though.

The union should **run training** for game workers moving on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Oh, that's almost comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to build a fair system, so there's no excuse. I'd push for credits, fair pay and a transition fund through the union, steadily, not in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I get to actually become good at this. I'd be a real localisation lead by 2030, with AI doing the grind and me doing the taste. I'd probably be fine until around 2034, then start moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride the tools and grow the collective with Inês, maybe hire a third person for Spanish. I'd invest the extra money in a second small flat, because rent has worked for me. And I'd keep the café as a someday plan for my mid-thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly excited. There's still an end date, but it feels far enough that I can enjoy the next bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a second flat and not shares or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I understand flats. My aunt's flat has paid my rent for three years and never once asked me to learn a new tool. Boring is good when everything else is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you hire someone, what would you tell them about the future of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth: they're joining for maybe six or seven good years. Then I'd pay them well enough to save for whatever comes next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to learn running a business before my main skill stops paying. What would help is a public income floor and cheap small-business loans for people starting in-person work, like cafés, workshops and care.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we lose culturally. When a machine localises every game, the jokes all start sounding the same. Somebody should notice when every grumpy blacksmith in every game talks exactly alike.

headlineQuote: When a machine localises every game, the jokes all start sounding the same.
portrait: Zoe is a 27-year-old **Portuguese-English** game localiser who uses AI drafts every day.
Rent from her **aunt's flat** covers her own rent, so she can take risks.
She shares a two-person **collective** with her friend Inês and backs a game workers' union.
Faced with fast AGI, she'd bet on a **board-game café**, using the robot delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to learn business before her skill stops paying.
whatWouldHelp: A **public income floor** for people losing creative work.
Cheap **small-business loans** for in-person work like cafés and workshops.
